red.focus: Explain legal meaning with reasons people can inspect
red.summary: Interpretation should not mean choosing whatever an official prefers. Learn to connect exact words, context and an applicable source to a conclusion.
checklist: I can state which words require interpretation
I can show relevant definitions and context
I can explain the result without relying on personal authority

sections.title: A Judge Must Give a Reason
sections.body_md: A resident asks whether a park rule permits bicycles. A judge's personal dislike of bicycles is not a legal explanation. The judge should identify the rule, definition and relevant context, then explain how those sources apply. The process does not guarantee everyone will agree, but it allows the conclusion to be inspected. This is a basic feature of law as reasoned governance rather than unaccountable personal power.

sections.title: Fair Notice Matters
sections.body_md: People organize their lives around legal language. If a rule is so obscure that ordinary affected persons cannot know what conduct is prohibited, serious fairness questions may arise under the governing legal order. Interpretation can sometimes clarify the text, but it cannot always cure a defect in how the rule was made or communicated. A legal adviser must distinguish the actual interpretive method from a policy argument that the rule should be rewritten.

sections.title: Speak So the Client Understands
sections.body_md: After interpreting a provision, explain what it means for the person's actual choices. Use necessary legal terms but define them in clear language. If more than one plausible reading exists, state the uncertainty and what might resolve it. A great lawyer does not use technical ambiguity to make a frightened client dependent on expertise. The purpose of legal interpretation is to make lawful obligations and protections understandable enough to guide responsible action.

yellow.focus: Recognize interpretation as an exercise of public power
yellow.summary: Judges, administrators and private arbiters interpret texts within different mandates. Learn why their source of authority matters for the legitimacy of a contested reading.
checklist: I can identify who is authorized to interpret a text
I can distinguish administrative guidance from a binding judgment
I can explain why consistency and reasons constrain discretion

sections.title: Not Every Interpreter Has the Same Role
sections.body_md: A regulator publishes guidance about a statute, while a court resolves a dispute over the statute's meaning. The guidance may be useful, but its binding effect depends on the legal system. A private adviser may offer a persuasive explanation without any authority to compel compliance. The reader must ask whose interpretation is controlling and why. This helps prevent public officials, advocates and courts from borrowing each other's authority simply because they use the same legal vocabulary.

sections.title: Consistency Protects Equality
sections.body_md: If identical legal language is interpreted differently for similarly situated people without a relevant reason, trust in the legal order can weaken. Precedent, published guidance, review and written reasons can constrain arbitrariness. The details differ by jurisdiction and institution. A sound interpretation should acknowledge earlier authoritative readings and explain justified distinctions or lawful change. Legal consistency does not require ignoring genuine differences in fact or amended law.

sections.title: Discretion Needs a Boundary
sections.body_md: An agency may have discretion to choose among lawful policies, but interpreting a statutory power is not the same as having unrestricted policy freedom. The governing text, procedural conditions and review standards define its mandate. A lawyer should identify where interpretation ends and discretionary decision-making begins. That boundary helps protect individuals from officials who claim the wording authorizes action the law never granted.

orange.focus: Compare interpretation, participation and minority protection
orange.summary: Different legal systems allocate interpretive power among courts, legislatures, administrators and communities. Examine when legal meaning can be contested by those whose lives it governs.
checklist: I can compare modes of constitutional and customary interpretation
I can identify procedural rights of affected persons
I can analyze the status of nonstate interpretive traditions

sections.title: Whose Interpretation Counts?
sections.body_md: A constitutional court, elected legislature and local customary institution may each articulate a rule affecting family or property relationships. Their legal force is not equal or automatic. A lawyer must identify the recognized sources and any rules governing conflict between them. At the same time, a comparative scholar should investigate how people within each community participate in interpretation. An account that records only the national court may miss the living legal practice it sought to govern.

sections.title: Affected Persons Need a Voice
sections.body_md: A rule on public benefits may be interpreted by officials without consulting recipients who understand its effects. Lawful notice, reasons, administrative review and participation can help expose mistaken assumptions. Such safeguards depend on the legal system; they should not be invented where absent. The ethical question nevertheless remains: what institutional arrangements allow affected people to contest the meaning imposed upon them? Interpretation has human consequences because it allocates rights and duties.

sections.title: Sacred Texts Require Respectful Specificity
sections.body_md: Religious legal traditions may draw on sacred writings, commentaries, juristic methods and communities of interpretation. Their status within state law varies, as do internal disagreements about meaning. A comparative lawyer should not assume a sacred passage functions like a statute in every jurisdiction or that one commentator speaks for all followers. Accurate analysis distinguishes theological authority, institutional recognition and enforceable positive law, while protecting the rights of persons affected by official interpretations.

black.focus: Defend interpretation as legitimate coercive reasoning
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate how legal meaning can be developed without disguising political preferences as textual certainty. Create safeguards against arbitrary interpretation and systematic exclusion.
checklist: I can distinguish lawful development from unauthorized rewriting
I can evaluate review and participation in interpretive institutions
I can defend transparent reason-giving under moral disagreement

sections.title: Meaning Can Be Contested Without Being Fiction
sections.body_md: A broadly worded legal guarantee may support more than one plausible application in a new technological setting. A responsible interpreter should identify the semantic possibilities, legal purpose, precedent and institutional mandate. Neither claiming mechanical certainty nor declaring unlimited judicial freedom is satisfactory. A doctoral theory must explain which considerations deserve weight and how a reviewing institution could detect error. Reasoned disagreement is compatible with law when its methods are public and constrained.

sections.title: Power Can Hide Behind Method
sections.body_md: An official may invoke 'original meaning' or 'purpose' to conceal a preferred political outcome while ignoring inconvenient evidence. Any interpretive method can be abused when its assumptions and sources are opaque. Transparent argument should state which texts, contexts and historical materials are accepted, why competing sources are rejected, and what institutional constraints apply. This openness is especially necessary where interpretation affects minority rights, liberty or legal status.

sections.title: Make Interpretation Accountable to People
sections.body_md: A legal system can protect legitimacy through accessible texts, published reasons, fair hearings, correction procedures and representative participation where appropriate. These safeguards cannot guarantee ideal outcomes, but they help prevent arbitrary exercises of authority. A doctoral scholar should evaluate the trade-off between consistency and needed legal development and specify mechanisms for review. The value of interpretation is measured ultimately by whether law offers intelligible, fair protection to people subject to its power.
